title: Python Overview & Development Environment
summary: Check your Python version and try interactive mode, script mode and venv, then use print(), input() and type conversion to finish a greeting program, a calculator and a BMI program.

lab1_setup.summary: Follow Lab 1 (set up your development environment) in this web lab. Check the Python version, try interactive mode (REPL), type() and type conversion, then create and activate a virtual environment .venv.
lab1_setup.notes: Installing VS Code and the Python extension, selecting the interpreter and creating a Google Colab notebook are steps you do on a real PC, outside the browser. The terminal in this lab plays the role of VS Code's built-in terminal (Ctrl+` / Cmd+`), and instead of the ▶ Run button you run a file with python3 filename.py. In the BusyBox shell the source command is written as . (a dot).
steps: This lab's Python is 3.14.10. Only the number differs from the 3.12.4 on the slides; what you learn is the same. On a Windows PC the command is usually python or py.

This feeds input into the REPL. After each >>> you see, in order, the value of the expression 5, the print output hi, and <class 'float'>. If you type just python3 yourself, the same >>> prompt appears, and exit() leaves it.
The five basic data types int, float, str, bool and NoneType are printed.
int(3.9) truncates rather than rounds, giving 3, and float(7) gives 7.0. Only 0, the empty string and None are False; 5 is True.
"3" + "3" is the concatenation 33; converted with int it is 6. Adding a string and an integer raises a TypeError, as in the last line (the start of the Traceback is hidden with grep).
"3.5" has to go through float to become the integer 3. Calling int("3.5") directly raises ValueError: invalid literal for int().
The virtual environment folder .venv is created, and activate and python appear inside bin. This lab has no pip, so --without-pip is added. On a real PC, python3 -m venv .venv is enough.

After activation, python points to ~/python-week1/.venv/bin/python; after deactivate it is /usr/bin/python again. If you activate it yourself without deactivate, (.venv) appears in front of the prompt.

hello.summary: Lab 2: print Hello, World! and Hello, Python!, store your name, major and date in variables and print them with labels, then pass several values to print() to make Week 1 of 16.
hello.notes: Fill in the TODOs with nano hello.py, press Ctrl+O (save) and Ctrl+X (exit), then run python3 hello.py again. Replace the name, major and date with your own.
steps: The starter code is only comments, so it prints nothing and exits normally (exit=0). Your task is to fill in the TODOs.
Output of the sample solution. Values passed with commas, as in print("Name:", name), are separated by one space each, and the last line is Week 1 of 16.
sep="-" changes the separator to give A-B, and end=" " puts a space instead of a newline, so the next print continues on the same line.
{name} inside the f-string is replaced by its value. :.1f gives one decimal place, and :, adds thousands separators (1,234,567).
As in the experiment on the slides, leaving out the closing quotation mark gives SyntaxError: unterminated string literal, and the ^ mark points to the problem. Not a single line of the program runs.

calc.summary: Lab 3: read two numbers with input(), convert them to float, and print their sum, difference, product and the quotient to two decimal places with f-strings.
steps: The inputs 8 and 2 are piped in beforehand. The starter code prints only the two prompts and no results. You can also run python3 calc.py yourself and type the numbers on the keyboard.
The input is not shown on screen, so the two prompts run together on one line. Because the values were converted to float, a decimal point appears, as in 8.0 + 2.0 = 10.0.
The quotient is 2.333..., but {a / b:.2f} shows it as 2.33.
Negative numbers work as well: -4.0, -8.0, -12.0, -3.00.
The three operators from the challenge: floor division 3.0, remainder 1.0, exponent 49.0. When both operands are floats, the result is a float too.

If the second number is 0, the sum, difference and product are printed, but the division stops with ZeroDivisionError: division by zero. Handling this is covered in the 'Files, Exceptions and JSON' chapter.

bmi.summary: Lab 4: read height (cm) and weight (kg), convert the height to m, and print BMI = weight ÷ height (m)² to one decimal place.
bmi.notes: The challenge, a BMI category (Underweight, Normal, Overweight, Obese), is built with if / elif / else from the 'Operators, Strings and Conditionals' chapter. Leave three test inputs and their expected results as comments at the bottom of the file.
steps: The starter code only reads the input and prints nothing.
These are the test values from the slides. You should see Height: 1.75 m, Weight: 70.0 kg, Your BMI is 22.9.
:.2f keeps the trailing zero, as in 1.60 m. In both cases the BMI is 25.0.
